title: The Mill on the Floss: A Literary Discussion

segments.title: Opening: The Mill and Its Masters

utterances.text: Welcome to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked — a close, searching conversation about one of the great novels in the English language.
George Eliot published this book in 1860, and it has never stopped asking uncomfortable questions.
About family, about money, about who gets to grow — and who gets crushed when they try.
I'm joined today by three extraordinary readers who each bring a completely different lens to this novel.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher whose passion is the architecture of great prose — how a sentence does its work, how an image earns its place.
There is no better guide to how Eliot builds her effects, line by line.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who specialises in the institutions that literature brings to life.
He knows what debt, respectability, and the law actually meant to people in the nineteenth century — and he will not let us sentimentalise it.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read this novel as a teenager and has been returning to it ever since.
She reads for the music of the thing — for what moves you, what makes you stop, what makes you read a sentence twice.

We're going to begin where every reading of this novel should begin — with the mill itself, and the family who runs it, and the forces that are already, from the very first pages, conspiring to break them.
What strikes me every time I return to this novel is how early Eliot establishes the idea of entrapment.
The mill is not just a setting — it is a mechanism.
It grinds, it processes, it turns living things into product.
And Eliot is extraordinarily deliberate about applying that metaphor to the human lives it contains — the Tullivers, ground down by forces they cannot name, let alone resist.
There is a passage that I think captures something essential about this — not about the mill directly, but about the moral world the Tullivers inhabit.
Eliot writes — and this is the narrator at her most quietly devastating —
"It is easy enough to spoil the lives of our neighbours without taking so much trouble; we can do it by lazy acquiescence and lazy omission, by trivial falsities for which we hardly know a reason."
That word — lazy — does so much work there.
Eliot is saying: the catastrophe doesn't require a villain. It only requires ordinary inattention.
Eleanor is right that inattention is the engine here — but I'd add that the social structures are designed to reward exactly that kind of inattention.
Tulliver is not undone by a conspiracy — he is undone by a dozen small negligences and a legal system that has no interest in protecting him.
Eliot gives us a full taxonomy of that process in the passage Eleanor just quoted.
The full sentence is worth hearing entire, because the accumulation is the point.
"by small frauds neutralised by small extravagances, by maladroit flatteries, and clumsily improvised insinuations."
"Clumsily improvised" — that is not the language of malice, it is the language of muddle.
And muddle, historically, is far more destructive than malice, because no one is ever held accountable for it.
What moves me about that passage — and it moves me every time — is how Eliot uses the word "we."
Not "they" — not pointing at the Tullivers or the Dodsons from a safe distance.
She says "we live from hand to mouth, most of us, with a small family of immediate desires."
She is indicting the reader alongside the characters.
That takes a kind of moral courage — or perhaps moral nerve — that I find breathtaking in a novelist.
And the human cost of all that muddle, as James puts it, lands hardest on Mr Tulliver himself.
There is a moment near the end of his life — a very short speech — that contains more than most novelists manage in a chapter.
He says to his wife and son — and I want to read this carefully —
"Give me a kiss, Bessy, and let us bear one another no ill-will; we shall never be young again — this world's been too many for me."
That phrase — "this world's been too many for me" — is about as undeceived as any character in fiction ever gets about their own defeat.
And yet Tom — his son — responds to that defeat not with grief but with demand.
Which brings us to one of the novel's most painful scenes, and the heart of what we want to explore today.
Tom Tulliver is the figure in this novel who most unsettles readers who want to assign simple moral verdicts.
He is not cruel in the way a tyrant is cruel — he is cruel in exactly the way Eliot diagnosed in that earlier passage: through rigid principle and narrow vision.
His confrontation with Maggie over Philip Wakem is the scene where that cruelty becomes fully visible.
He says to her — and he means every word of this, which is what makes it so devastating —
"I can't trust you, Maggie. There is no consistency in you."
And then — and this is where I think Eliot wants us to feel the full weight of his self-righteousness —
"while I have been contriving and working that my father may have some peace of mind before he dies — working for the respectability of our family — you have done all you can to destroy both."
He genuinely believes he is the injured party.
And that belief — that absolute self-certainty — is in its own way one of the most damaging forces in the novel.
What Eliot does structurally there is extraordinary — she lets Tom indict himself through the very grammar of his accusation.
Notice the parallel construction: "I have been contriving and working" — active, effortful — set against "you have done all you can to destroy."
He has cast himself as builder and Maggie as demolisher — in a single sentence that he thinks is rational accusation but is actually pure self-portrait.
And Eliot is too good a writer to tell us that — she lets the syntax show us.
I want to go back for a moment to the father — because Mr Tulliver's line shadows everything Tom says after it.
"This world's been too many for me" — that is a man who has given up the fiction of control.
Tom has inherited all of his father's pride and none of his father's capacity for tenderness.
So where the father reaches out to say "give me a kiss, Bessy," the son reaches for a Bible and demands an oath.
That contrast — I find it almost unbearable.
That contrast will be at the very centre of everything we discuss today.
The tenderness that breaks through, the rigidity that destroys, and the one character — Maggie — caught between them.
In our next segment we'll look much more closely at Maggie herself — at what Eliot gives her, and what the novel, and the world of the novel, withholds.

segments.title: Maggie's Forbidden Library: Intellect Against Convention

utterances.text: Welcome back to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
Today we're going deep into something that sits at the heart of this novel: Maggie Tulliver's mind.
Her extraordinary, unsatisfied, half-wild intellect — and what the world around her does with it.
With me are three people who have thought long and hard about this novel.
Dr Eleanor Hartley teaches creative writing and is fascinated by the architecture of fiction — how a novelist builds her effects from the inside out.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who brings the real context — what these institutions actually meant, who they protected, and who they crushed.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has loved this novel since she was a teenager and has never quite recovered.
The question before us today: what does George Eliot show us about a brilliant child in a world that has no place for her brilliance?
What strikes me first is how Eliot frames Maggie's intelligence as something the narrator herself has to apologise for — but with a completely straight face.
There's this marvellous passage where the narrator steps back and surveys the territory of Maggie's mind.
"in travelling over her small mind you would have found the most unexpected ignorance as well as unexpected knowledge."
That word "small" is doing extraordinary work there.
It's simultaneously condescending and tender — this miniature landscape that turns out to contain depths you never expected.
And the catalogue that follows — she can define polygamy, she has deduced what "poly" means from first principles — is genuinely astonishing for an eight-year-old.
But she has no idea that gypsies need groceries. The gap between the abstract and the practical is total.
And that gap is exactly what makes her run-away-to-the-gypsies scheme so perfect.
The resolution she forms is wonderfully, painfully Maggie.
Eliot gives us her interior logic so precisely — the gypsies will receive her gladly on account of her "superior knowledge."
She is going to be a queen among people who will finally appreciate what she knows.
And then the narrator gives us the bare statement of her plan:
"No! she would run away and go to the gypsies, and Tom should never see her any more."
That exclamation mark at the start — that's a whole child.
It's worth pausing on why the gypsies specifically — because it isn't random.
Maggie has been told, repeatedly, that she is "like a gypsy" and "half wild."
That's her family and community telling her she doesn't fit — that her energy, her darkness, her unruliness, place her outside respectable society.
So her logic is impeccable, really: if I belong nowhere here, perhaps I belong there.
The tragedy is that the "there" she imagines is entirely a projection of her own longing — it has nothing to do with actual Romani life, which she knows precisely nothing about.
And the collapse of that fantasy is one of the great comic-gothic sequences in nineteenth-century fiction.
Within minutes of arriving, Maggie's mind has rewritten the whole scene in the most lurid possible terms.
"she had begun to think that they meant perhaps to kill her as soon as it was dark, and cut up her body for gradual cooking."
"Gradual cooking" — I have never recovered from that phrase.
It's the imagination of a child who has read too much and experienced too little — which is exactly Eliot's point about her education.
The same mind that deduced the meaning of "poly" from pure etymology now deduces that the old man with fierce eyes must be the Devil in disguise.
What undoes me every time is the detail about not wanting to offend the gypsies by letting them see her unfavourable opinion of them.
She thinks she may be about to be eaten — and her primary concern is social embarrassment.
That is such a precise portrait of a certain kind of anxious, over-socialised intelligence.
And it connects directly back to what drives her away in the first place — the anguish of Tom preferring Lucy.
The narrator is almost surgical about how jealousy transforms her: she would have thought a little while ago she could never be cross with Lucy.
"Maggie would have thought a little while ago that she could never be cross with pretty little Lucy, any more than she could be cruel to a little white mouse."
The white mouse — that image is so small and so exact.
The Lucy and Tom dynamic here is also a social lesson Maggie is being taught without anyone intending to teach it.
Tom is suddenly attentive to Lucy in a way he never was before — and Lucy is fair, neat, passive, pretty.
Maggie is dark, untidy, clever, and difficult.
The nine-year-old is already being shown which kind of girl gets rewarded — and it is not her kind.
Which makes the Tom-at-school passage all the more poignant — because Tom actually misses her mind.
He cannot admit it in those terms, but the evidence is there.
Maggie has been pestering Mr Stelling with questions about the Roman Empire, and the narrator gives us Tom's reward from this:

"he had actually come to a dim understanding of the fact that there had once been people upon the earth who were so fortunate as to know Latin without learning it through the medium of the Eton Grammar."
"A dim understanding" — Eliot can barely keep the laughter out of the prose.
But it is also genuinely moving — Maggie has cracked open Tom's world a fraction, without either of them knowing it.
And that luminous idea — that people once spoke Latin naturally — is described as a great addition to his historical acquirements, which were otherwise confined to an epitomised history of the Jews.
Eliot is quietly devastating about the poverty of Tom's formal education compared to Maggie's chaotic self-instruction.
Tom has a proper schoolmaster, Latin grammar, a structured curriculum — and his historical understanding fits in a paragraph.
Maggie has a dictionary and whatever she can grab — and she's reconstructing etymology from first principles at age eight.
And yet nobody in Maggie's world can afford to give her that knowledge properly.
There is a moment later in the novel where Mr Tulliver speaks to Maggie, and what he says carries everything — all the weight of what this family cannot give her.
"Ay, my little wench, but I shall never live twice o'er."
There's no bitterness in it — just finality.
He loves her. He cannot help her.
That line stays with you.
The intelligence is there — it's dazzling, it's real — and the world simply does not have a shape for it.
In our next segment, we'll look at what happens when that intelligence meets the wider world — education, money, and the institutions that define who gets to know things.

segments.title: The Social Machine: Class, Commerce, and Ruin

utterances.text: Welcome back to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
Today we're diving into something that sits at the very heart of this novel — the machinery of class, commerce, and ruin.
George Eliot is fascinated by the way social forces grind people down — and by the strange human pride that either resists or colludes in that grinding.
With me are three guests who have been thinking hard about exactly these questions.
Dr Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who reads Eliot with a craftsperson's eye — always asking how the architecture of a sentence does its work.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian — the person you want in the room when the novel turns to courts, debt, and the institutions that shape a life.
And Ms Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has lived with this novel since she was a teenager — she brings the reader's visceral, intimate response.
Let's begin with Mr Tulliver's extraordinary letter to Mrs Glegg — a gesture so perfectly self-defeating it's almost operatic.
What Eliot does in that scene is structurally breathtaking, and I mean that literally — breathtaking as a comic device.
We've just spent several paragraphs inside Mrs Glegg's satisfaction at her own magnanimity — her sense of how graciously she is about to forgive.
Eliot has inflated that balloon with great care.
Then Tulliver's letter arrives — and she lets it pop with a single, devastating clause.
Listen to the precision of what Tulliver actually writes — and Eliot quotes it almost verbatim through the narrator's paraphrase.
"She was welcome to his house whenever she liked to come, but he desired no favours from her, either for himself or his children."
That word 'welcome' — doing all the work of surface civility — and then 'no favours' cutting clean through it.
It's a sentence built like a trap: the door held open with one hand, the other hand raised in refusal.
And it is worth pausing on what 'no favours' means in material terms here.
Five hundred pounds in the 1820s or 1830s — which is roughly when Eliot sets these events — represents a very significant sum, a year's income for a prosperous tradesman, perhaps more.
Mrs Glegg has lent this money to her own brother-in-law — lending within the family was entirely ordinary — but so was using that debt as leverage.
The Dodson family operates on a principle of accountancy applied to kinship — every obligation recorded, every favour tallied.
When Tulliver says he wants no favours, he is declaring independence from that entire system of mutual moral debt.
The tragedy — and it is tragic, not just comic — is that he cannot actually afford to make that declaration.
What gets me is the narrator's tone in setting all of this up.
'Mrs Glegg being in this state of satisfaction in her own lofty magnanimity, I leave you to judge' — that 'I leave you to judge' is delicious.
Eliot steps forward and gives us a little wink, without ever breaking the composure of the prose.
And then the word 'lofty' — applied to Mrs Glegg's self-satisfaction — is doing something almost cruel.
Loftiness implies height, elevation, virtue — but here it's a posture, not a quality.
Eliot respects Mrs Glegg, in a sense — but she never lets her off the hook.
That connects beautifully to the camel's back passage, which I think is one of Eliot's most quietly outrageous pieces of satirical architecture.
She introduces Mrs Tulliver's influence over her husband with this marvellous proviso — that women always incline a man to do what she wishes, or the reverse.
Which means, of course, that women always influence men — just sometimes in the opposite direction from what they intend.
And then the camel's back simile arrives — and Eliot immediately complicates it, forensically.
"It might even be comparable to that proverbial feather which has the credit or discredit of breaking the camel's back."
'Credit or discredit' — in one little phrase she unpacks the entire double-edged moral ambiguity of being that final, decisive feather.
And then she immediately exonerates the feather by pointing to all the other feathers that came before.
It's a miniature essay on causation — and on the injustice of assigning blame to the final link in a long chain.
And the chain in this case is Mr Tulliver's mounting legal obsessions — above all his fixation on Wakem.
The portrait of Wakem in the next passage is fascinating from a legal history perspective.
What we see is not actually a corrupt lawyer — we see a competent one, viewed through the eyes of a man who mistakes competence for malice.
Tulliver has a principle — 'water was water' — which he regards as self-evidently decisive.
He cannot comprehend that the law may have its own internal logic quite indifferent to natural justice as he conceives it.
And Eliot gives us Tulliver's hatred of Wakem with this wonderful, snarling sentence.
"A hook-nosed glib fellow! as cool as a cucumber, — always looking so sure of his game!"
That's not the narrator speaking — that's Tulliver's interior voice, rendered in free indirect discourse with almost journalistic accuracy.
The prejudice — including the physical prejudice of 'hook-nosed' — is presented without authorial endorsement but with complete imaginative sympathy for how that mind works.
The 'cool as a cucumber' line always stops me — because it's exactly the right register for Tulliver's rage.
He's a hot man — impulsive, all heat and pride — and what infuriates him most is a cold adversary who simply cannot be rattled.
But then I think — this is the world Maggie is born into.
Her father's pride driving the family toward ruin, the Dodson machinery clanking away — and Maggie has no power in any of it.
There's a passage about Maggie as a young girl — after she's been found fault with, again — that breaks my heart every single time.
"There is no hopelessness so sad as that of early youth, when the soul is made up of wants, and has no long memories, no superadded life in the life of others."
'The soul is made up of wants.' Six words.
That is the whole of childhood poverty — not just material poverty, but the poverty of having enormous needs and no framework yet to bear them.
And 'no superadded life in the life of others' — that phrase is doing something structurally that I find extraordinary.
Eliot is describing what maturity actually gives you — memory, accumulated sympathy, the ability to hold your present suffering inside a longer story.
Children — and Maggie here as a child — have none of that scaffolding.
And crucially, Eliot says we who look on 'think lightly' of the child's despair — because our own accumulated life means we can imagine it passing.
But to the child, there is no future lightening things — there is only the present darkness.
That is the cruelest structural irony in the whole novel — the narrator has the perspective Maggie lacks, and yet perspective is precisely what cannot be shared.
What interests me is how that hopelessness compounds as Maggie gets older — and how the social machine tightens around her precisely as her wants become more complex.
By the time we reach the crisis with Stephen Guest — chapter fifty-two — we're watching a woman who has been shaped by deprivation and duty in almost equal measure.
The narrator gives us a remarkable, almost clinical account of that internal battle.
'All the worst evil in her had lain in ambush till now, and had suddenly started up full-armed, with hideous, overpowering strength.'
'Full-armed' is the word that arrests me — it's Miltonic, almost epic, applied to a desire she has never before admitted.
And the question she asks herself — 'who had renounced anything for her?' — is the question the novel has been building toward from the beginning.
And yet she doesn't take the escape.
The image Eliot gives for why not is one of the most arresting in the book — and I find it almost painful to read aloud.
"She might as well hope to enjoy walking by maiming her feet, as hope to enjoy an existence in which she set out by maiming the faith and sympathy that were the best organs of her soul."
'Best organs of her soul' — it's almost anatomical.
As if sympathy and fidelity are not virtues but working parts — remove them and you don't become free, you become broken.
I have friends who think Maggie should have simply gone with Stephen and be done with it.
But that image answers them: she is not choosing duty over happiness — she is recognising that the happiness on offer would destroy the self doing the choosing.
And then Tom's condemnation arrives — and it is, formally, one of the most brutal passages in Victorian fiction.
Every sentence is short.
Every sentence hits like a hammer blow.
Listen to the rhythm of what Tom actually says.
"You have disgraced us all. You have disgraced my father's name. You have been a curse to your best friends."
Three parallel 'you have' constructions — the anaphora of accusation.
He then says: 'I wash my hands of you forever. You don't belong to me.'
'You don't belong to me' — ending on a denial of kinship rather than a declaration of rejection — is somehow worse than anything that came before it.
Tom is the social machine speaking at its most unmediated.
Respectable Victorian society had very clear protocols for how a woman in Maggie's position — compromised, returned, unrepentant in her interiority — was to be handled.
She is to be expelled from the family unit, which is itself a legal and economic entity with a reputation to protect.
Tom is not simply being cruel — he genuinely believes he is doing what duty requires.
And that is what makes this scene so much harder than simple villainy.
Tom is what Mr Tulliver's world has succeeded in producing — a man with pride, with the work ethic, with the moral vocabulary of respectability — and it destroys his sister.
And he doesn't even see it.
That is the unbearable thing.
He speaks with complete certainty — 'I wash my hands of you forever' — as if those words cost him nothing.
We who have been reading know what Maggie is — the ferocity of her interior life, the depth of her loyalty, all that maimed but unbroken sympathy.
And Tom looks at all that and sees only disgrace.
That moment — 'you don't belong to me' — might be the most precise summary of everything the novel has been arguing about belonging, class, and the limits of family.
We've moved from Mr Tulliver's proud, self-defeating letter all the way to this — the ruin not just of finances but of kinship itself.
In our next segment, we'll turn to the texture of Eliot's language — the way the style itself carries the novel's moral weight.

segments.title: Close Reading: Comic Interludes and Hidden Pain

utterances.text: Welcome back to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
In this segment we're turning to something George Eliot does with remarkable precision: the comic interlude that carries hidden pain.
The laughter in this novel is never simple.
Caroline Woodcourt has been our close reader throughout this episode — someone who came to this novel as a teenager and has returned to it again and again.
She's brought us passages today that range from pastoral tenderness to biting social satire.
Eleanor Hartley is here with her novelist's eye for how these effects are built.
And James Blackstone will remind us what the social world outside the novel's pages actually looked like.
Caroline, let's start with Tom and Maggie by the river.
This passage stops me every single time I read it.
There's such a pure, uncomplicated happiness in it — and yet the whole novel is already gathering behind it like a storm.
The narrator gives us a sentence that is almost heartbreaking in its innocence.

"They trotted along and sat down together, with no thought that life would ever change much for them; they would only get bigger and not go to school, and it would always be like the holidays; they would always live together and be fond of each other."
That word "always" — it appears twice in that one sentence, and each time it lands like a small, tender lie.
They won't always live together. Life will change beyond any imagining.
Eliot plants the flood in this passage too — the Eagre described as a hungry monster, the Great Ash that groaned like a man.
The gothic is already present inside the pastoral, even in the children's happiest morning.
What Caroline identifies there is one of Eliot's most precise structural techniques.
She builds the idyll from the inside out — listing the mill, the chestnut tree, the Ripple, the Floss — accumulating sensation.
And then she plants the monster right in the middle of it: the Eagre, the groaning tree.
The children aren't frightened by those things — they're thrilled by them.
Which is exactly right for childhood — the gothic and the pastoral aren't opposites, they're the same landscape.
And then there's that extraordinary detail: Maggie reading about Christiana crossing the river and always seeing the Floss.
The river she imagines as the passage to death is her own river. The novel tells you everything in one image.
What strikes me, reading this alongside the other childhood passage, is how much the physical landscape is doing.
Tom thinks people were at a disadvantage who lived anywhere else on the globe.
That's not just sentiment — that's the psychology of a provincial mill-owner's son in the 1820s and 30s.
The mill, the land, the river — these are economic as well as emotional facts.
And the loss of them, which is coming, will be both.
Which brings us to the other childhood passage, the one about Tom's face — and this is where Eliot's irony becomes almost mischievous.
Tom is described as one of those lads that look, at twelve or thirteen, exactly like goslings.
Light-brown hair, cream-and-roses cheeks, indeterminate nose. Nothing there, apparently.
But then the narrator turns the whole thing around.
"Under these average boyish physiognomies that she seems to turn off by the gross, she conceals some of her most rigid, inflexible purposes, some of her most unmodifiable characters."
"Turn off by the gross" — it's a manufacturing metaphor, perfect for a novel set around a mill.
And "unmodifiable" — that's a word that sounds almost bureaucratic, which is exactly the point.
Tom's character is fixed, irrevocable — and the joke of the gosling face is that nobody can read it there.
That passage is one of the great sleights of hand in nineteenth-century fiction.
Eliot begins by apparently reassuring us: Maggie is the distinctive one, the legible one.
Nature has moulded and coloured her face with decided intention — you can read her.
And then she says: no, actually, that's exactly where Nature is most deceptive.
The "dark-eyed, demonstrative, rebellious girl" may turn out passive compared with the pink-and-white indeterminate boy.
Which is, of course, partly true and partly devastatingly wrong about both of them.
Eliot won't let you settle. She keeps undercutting the very generalizations she's making.
There's also a quietly radical argument about gender being made there.
The assumption being undermined is precisely the Victorian one: that legibility and demonstrativeness in a woman signal her true nature.
Physiognomy was taken seriously — not just as folk wisdom, but as a quasi-scientific claim about reading faces and character.
Eliot dismantles it in one paragraph, with the comic apparatus of the gosling comparison doing most of the heavy work.
Now — the mud scene.
This is perhaps the most extraordinary single passage in the book for the ratio of comedy to catastrophe.
Eliot invokes Aristotle — the Greek term τι μέγεθος, the greatness of scale required for tragedy — in a scene about a child pushing another child into mud.
Let me read it, because it needs to be heard whole.

"There were passions at war in Maggie at that moment to have made a tragedy, if tragedies were made by passion only; but the essential τι μέγεθος which was present in the passion was wanting to the action; the utmost Maggie could do, with a fierce thrust of her small brown arm, was to push poor little pink-and-white Lucy into the cow-trodden mud."
"Poor little pink-and-white Lucy." It's devastating and it's funny at exactly the same moment.
The tragedy is real — the passions are real — but the scale of the action available to a seven-year-old girl is a muddy shove.
The craft in that sentence is astonishing.
Eliot holds the elevated register — tragedy, passion, the Greek philosophical term — for the entire first clause.
And then she detonates it: "the cow-trodden mud."
The bathos is surgical — the gap between the Aristotelian scale and the actual event is exactly the size of Maggie's tragedy throughout the whole novel.
She always has the interior magnitude. The world never gives her the commensurate action.
And notice what Maggie pushes: Lucy.
Lucy, who is pink-and-white — the same phrase Eliot used for Tom in the physiognomy passage.
The socially legible, the conventionally lovely, the readable — that is what Maggie assaults.
It is not accidental that Lucy ends up in the mud and Maggie ends up in disgrace.
The same dynamic plays out at every scale, including the novel's ending.
From mud to muslin — Bob Jakin's sales pitch to Mrs Glegg is one of the great comic set-pieces.
Bob is conducting what I can only describe as a masterclass in reverse salesmanship.
He tells Mrs Glegg that there's no point in her looking at the figured muslin.
"You might as well look at poor folks's victual, mum; it 'ud on'y take away your appetite."
He's shaming her into buying it. By telling her it's too good for her — and simultaneously too damaged to be worth her time.
He even throws it behind him on the turf, "to save Mrs Glegg's eyes."
The whole scene plays like a comic turn — and yet Bob genuinely loves the Tulliver family. His comedy is also loyalty.
What's so good about Bob's voice is its texture.
Eliot renders dialect phonetically throughout — the dropped consonants, the distorted vowels — without condescension.
Bob is far more cunning than anyone gives him credit for — you can hear it in the construction of each sentence.
"The Princess Victoree might ha' worn" this muslin. And then he tosses it on the turf.
He's playing Mrs Glegg like an instrument. And she's probably aware of it and delighted anyway.
Bob Jakin represents a real social type: the itinerant packman, operating between manufacturing and retail, outside the established commercial structure.
He has no shop, no ledger, no credit — he carries damaged and second-hand goods, and his capital is entirely verbal.
The joke about poor folks's victual is also a class joke with real teeth: Bob knows exactly where his goods come from, and where they're going.
Ten shillings for ten yards. The huckster's wife at Fibb's End. Those are real economic facts, not local colour.
And then we arrive at what I think is the darkest comedy in the entire novel: the St Ogg's passage.
Eliot imagines the alternative history: what if Maggie had returned from her drift with Stephen as Mrs Stephen Guest?
She states the principle flatly.
"We judge others according to results; how else?—not knowing the process by which results are arrived at."
Then she dramatizes it in that extraordinary long sentence about what people would have said — the one that mimics the voice of gossiping opinion.
"And a deformed young man, you know! — and young Guest so very fascinating."
It's devastating. Philip Wakem disposed of in a parenthesis. Society's entire moral framework condensed to a bracket.
The technique there is free indirect discourse at its most savage.
Eliot inhabits the voice of St Ogg's opinion so completely that for a moment you can't quite tell where the narrator ends and the gossip begins.
"Public opinion, in these cases, is always of the feminine gender — not the world, but the world's wife."
That phrase — "the world's wife" — it carries contempt and pity in equal measure, and it's directed at women by a woman writer.
Eliot knows she's writing for and against that audience simultaneously.
There's a legal precision to the phrase "not knowing the process by which results are arrived at" that I don't think is accidental.
The word "culpability" appears immediately before it: she had not eloped to be married — which came to the same thing, "so far as her culpability was concerned."
Culpability is a legal term. It belongs in a courtroom.
And the tribunal Eliot is describing — St Ogg's, the world's wife — has exactly that function: it pronounces judgment, it determines consequences.
It just does so without any of the procedural safeguards a court would theoretically have.
And the last sentence of that passage is almost thrown away — and absolutely cuts.
Miss Unit — who declares she will never visit Mr and Mrs Stephen Guest on moral grounds — is dismissed in one clause.
"My belief is, that Miss Unit had no cards sent her."
That's the whole moral of St Ogg's in nine words: moral principle is just social exclusion with better excuses.
What strikes me, listening to all of this, is that the comedy and the pain are never separate in Eliot — they're the same instrument.
From Tom and Maggie sitting happily by the Floss, to Maggie and the mud, to Bob and the muslin, to Miss Unit's uninvited state — the irony is always doing moral work.
Thank you all. In the next segment we'll be looking at how Eliot handles time — memory, loss, and the impossibility of going back.

segments.title: Brother and Sister: The Fracture Deepens

utterances.text: Welcome back to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
We've been tracing the relationship between Tom and Maggie Tulliver — that bond which is, in many ways, the beating heart of this novel.
In this segment, we're focusing on a moment that is both quietly comic and genuinely heartbreaking — Tom away at school, failing, and reduced to a kind of private desperation.
Eleanor Hartley is here — novelist, creative writing teacher, and someone who reads sentences the way a watchmaker reads mechanisms.
James Blackstone brings us the social and institutional world — what school actually meant for a boy like Tom, and what was at stake in getting it wrong.
And Caroline Woodcourt, who has lived with this novel since adolescence, and who I suspect knows exactly what it feels like to pray your way through an impossible Latin declension.
Eleanor, let's begin with you — there's a remarkable sentence near the start of this passage.
George Eliot writes that under this vigorous schoolroom treatment, Tom became more like a girl than he had ever been in his life before.
What's she doing there — structurally, I mean?
It's a provocation, isn't it — right at the top of the paragraph.
Eliot places that phrase — 'more like a girl' — knowing full well it will snag the reader's attention, possibly irritate them.
But then she immediately unpacks what she means — and the unpacking is everything.
She's talking about a kind of susceptibility — pride that has no comfortable resting place, that meets only bruises.
The structural move is brilliant: she uses a culturally loaded comparison to open a door, and then walks you through it into something much more precise and compassionate.
She's also, quietly, indicting the education system — Mr Stelling's world has made Tom feel 'uncouth and stupid.'
And that verdict doesn't come from Tom — it comes from the narrator, who sees the cruelty of a standard imposed on the wrong boy.
That institutional dimension is worth sitting with for a moment.
A boy like Tom — the son of a miller, destined for trade — had no earthly use for Latin supines or Euclid.
The curriculum Stelling imposes was designed for a different class entirely — for boys who would go to university, read law, enter the church.
Eliot actually diagnoses this directly — Stelling, she tells us elsewhere, has a ready-made opinion that all minds are alike and that the classical curriculum is the universal education.
It's a form of institutional violence — gentle, credentialed, entirely self-assured, and deeply damaging.
And Eliot understood it in her bones — she was a woman who had educated herself ferociously because no institution would properly educate her.
What moves me most in this passage is the moment Tom decides to pray.
Because Eliot is so precise about the texture of his hesitation — he 'shrank from the novelty and irregularity' of an extempore prayer.
He's a child who has learned forms, who trusts structures, and now he's in a place where no form fits what he needs.
And then the prayer itself arrives — and it is one of the most tender things in the novel.
"and please to make me always remember my Latin"
That 'always' — it's heartbreaking.
He's not asking for it once or for tomorrow — he's asking to be permanently transformed into the kind of boy who can hold Latin in his head.
And Euclid — the way she handles Euclid is where it tips into something almost comic, but never loses the pathos.
She shows Tom actually deliberating — 'whether he should ask to see what it meant, or whether there was any other mental state which would be more applicable to the case.'
He's applying the same dogged, practical logic to prayer that he applies to everything.
And then the resolution — and this is the structural punchline — he doesn't ask to understand Euclid.
"And make Mr Stelling say I sha'n't do Euclid any more. Amen."
The solution is to remove the obstacle, not to conquer it.
It's a child's perfectly rational response to an irrational imposition — and Eliot renders it without a trace of condescension.
There's something else in that prayer that I keep returning to.
Before the Latin petition, we're told Tom prays for his parents and 'little sister' — and that he had begun to pray for Maggie when she was a baby.
The narrator gives us that almost as a parenthetical — and yet it changes everything in the scene.
Because we're watching Tom at his most reduced — humiliated, desperate, privately pleading — and even here, Maggie is present.
The bond between them is encoded into the very form of his nightly prayers — it predates language, almost.
That's what makes the eventual fracture between them so painful to read.
Eliot has given us this — Tom alone in the dark, whispering Maggie's name into his prayers — so that we understand the depth of what is later broken.
She's a very long-game novelist.
Every tender detail is also a future wound.
Every tender detail is also a future wound — I think that might be the motto of this entire novel.
In our next segment, we'll turn to Maggie herself — to what this schooling period, seen from her side, reveals about how differently the world is calibrated for a girl with her kind of mind.

segments.title: Eliot's Technique: How Voice Shapes Judgment

utterances.text: Welcome to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked, the show where we spend serious time with one of the most extraordinary novels in the English language.
I'm joined today by three guests who each bring a distinct lens to George Eliot's work.
Dr Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher whose great passion is the architecture of prose — how sentences are built to carry meaning, image by image.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who keeps us honest about the real world behind the fiction — the institutions, the law, what poverty and class actually meant.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has read this novel more times than she'd probably care to admit, and who cares deeply about what it feels like to be inside it.
Today we're looking at something that runs through every page of this novel: how Eliot's narrative voice shapes the way we judge her characters.
Eleanor, I want to start with you, because the very opening of this book does something technically audacious.
What is Eliot actually doing with her narrator in those first pages?
What she's doing is setting a trap — a very elegant, very deliberate one.
The novel opens in what feels like pure present-tense observation — the mill, the river, the child on the bank.
We believe we're there. We believe we're watching.
And then Eliot pulls back the curtain with this extraordinary moment of bodily awakening.
She writes — and I want to read this exactly as it stands —

"Ah, my arms are really benumbed. I have been pressing my elbows on the arms of my chair, and dreaming that I was standing on the bridge in front of Dorlcote Mill, as it looked one February afternoon many years ago."
The physical detail of the benumbed arms is genius — it grounds the narrator in a body, in a chair, in the present.
Everything we have just experienced as vivid reality is retroactively revealed as reverie.
And the effect is to make memory itself feel like the most real thing in the novel.
What I find so striking is the intimacy of that "Ah."
It's not a literary throat-clearing. It's the sound of someone genuinely startled back into their own body.
And from that single syllable, we understand that this narrator has a relationship with that mill that is personal, unresolved, still charged.
It does something I think no amount of third-person narration could do as quickly: it gives us access to longing.
And then the whole novel is going to be about longing, in one form or another.
I want to add something that Eleanor's point opens up, which is the question of whose memory this is and what work it performs.
The narrator here is not a neutral recording device. She is an interested party, somebody for whom the mill carries emotional weight.
And that has a very specific effect on our relationship to the judgment the novel will later make of its characters.
We are being asked to see Maggie's world through a narrator who already loves it — who has dreamt herself back into it.
That is not objectivity. That is — with full authorial intention — sympathy as method.
James has put his finger on something crucial — and it connects directly to the passage where Eliot meditates on childhood memory and what she calls the ease of familiar scenes.
This is the narrator at her most philosophically exposed, and I think it's one of the great passages in the novel.
She writes —

"There is no sense of ease like the ease we felt in those scenes where we were born, where objects became dear to us before we had known the labour of choice, and where the outer world seemed only an extension of our own personality."
"The labour of choice" — that phrase does so much in three words.
It implies that adult consciousness is a kind of burden, a perpetual weighing and judging that childhood is mercifully free of.
And when you set that alongside the narrator's waking moment at the start of the novel, you see the whole project: Eliot is trying to recover something that by its nature cannot be recovered.
The sentence doesn't stop there, and the continuation is even more beautiful to me.
She goes on to say that our affections have a trick of twining round old inferior things.
"If our affections had not a trick of twining round those old inferior things; if the loves and sanctities of our life had no deep immovable roots in memory."
"Twining" — it's such a physical word, almost botanical.
And then "deep immovable roots" — the metaphor shifts from vine to tree and the effect is one of absolute groundedness, something that cannot be argued out of existence.
That is exactly the emotional case being made for Maggie, before Maggie herself has even entered the argument.
Though I'd note there's a subtle irony in that passage which Eliot is far too intelligent to leave unacknowledged.
She mocks the idea of upward-striving taste — "an improved taste in upholstery scorns it" — and then deploys one of the most brilliant satirical asides in the novel.

"Is not the striving after something better and better in our surroundings the grand characteristic that distinguishes man from the brute, or, to satisfy a scrupulous accuracy of definition, that distinguishes the British man from the foreign brute?"
The sting is in "scrupulous accuracy of definition."
That is the voice of a narrator who is simultaneously inside the sentimental argument and watching it from outside with considerable amusement.
The same voice that shapes how we feel about Tom, about Maggie, about every moral verdict the novel asks us to reach.
And that question of moral verdict brings us, inevitably, to the confrontation between Tom and Philip — where the narrator's technique of shaping judgment becomes almost uncomfortably powerful.
Eleanor, you've been looking closely at the scene where Tom faces down Philip Wakem.
This scene is technically fascinating because Eliot gives Tom a speech that is, in its own brutal terms, entirely coherent.
Tom believes every word. He is not performing cruelty — he is exercising what he understands as protection.
And Eliot lets him make his case in direct speech, without immediate authorial comment.
He says —
"I'll save her from throwing herself away on you, — from making herself a laughing-stock, — from being flouted by a man like your father, because she's not good enough for his son."
"You know well enough what sort of justice and cherishing you were preparing for her."
The word "cherishing" there is devastating — Tom deploys it with contempt, as if tenderness itself were a form of deception.
And yet the narrator withholds editorializing at precisely the moment we most want to be told how to feel.
That withholding is agonizing as a reader, because you know exactly how Eliot feels — and yet she trusts you to feel it yourself.
And then the narrator shifts to Maggie's room, and the technique changes entirely.
Now we're inside Maggie's consciousness — and the narration becomes acutely, almost unbearably physical.
Eliot writes —

"Her heart bled for Philip; she went on recalling the insults that had been flung at him with so vivid a conception of what he had felt under them, that it was almost like a sharp bodily pain to her."
"Making her beat the floor with her foot and tighten her fingers on her palm."
The beating foot, the tightened fingers — these are details you don't invent; you observe them.
They place Maggie's empathy in her body before they place it in her mind, and that is how you make a reader feel rather than merely understand.
And what is particularly ruthless — in the best possible sense — is what Eliot reveals about Maggie's interior conflict in that same passage.
She had believed herself at peace, above the fray.
Eliot records the collapse of that belief with perfect precision —

"She used to think in that time that she had made great conquests, and won a lasting stand on serene heights above worldly temptations and conflict. And here she was down again in the thick of a hot strife."
"Serene heights" to "hot strife" — four syllables to three — the fall is in the rhythm.
The narrator doesn't tell us Maggie has failed her own ideals. The language enacts it.
James, that is exactly right — and it connects to something that happens later, when Dr Kenn is left alone, trying to find a path through an impossible situation.
Because there Eliot shifts technique again — now we're in free indirect discourse for a man trying to think ethically, and the narration is extraordinarily scrupulous.
The narrator tells us that for Dr Kenn — and this is the pivot of the entire passage —
"her conscience must not be tampered with; the principle on which she had acted was a safer guide than any balancing of consequences."
That phrase, "balancing of consequences," is a quiet but devastating critique of purely consequentialist ethics — from inside a character's thought, not the narrator's own voice.
Eliot is using Kenn's admiration for Maggie to make the moral case she cannot quite make on Maggie's own behalf without tipping into special pleading.
It's also — and I think this matters — a deeply compassionate act toward the reader.
By that point in the novel you may be furious at Maggie, or heartbroken for her, or both at once.
And Eliot doesn't resolve that. She gives you a man she clearly respects, standing with his hands behind his back, looking at the carpet, unable to find the answer.
That is the narrator saying: this is hard. It should be hard. Your confusion is the appropriate response.
Sympathy as method, judgment without editorializing, conscience over consequences — these are the tools Eliot is deploying through every modulation of her narrator's voice.
In our next segment we'll be turning to the world outside the novel — the social and legal realities that give these characters their particular gravity and their particular constraints.
James, I suspect you've been waiting for that.

segments.title: Closing: The Weight of What Cannot Be Undone

utterances.text: We've been tracing the threads of this novel through its social world, its family tensions, its remarkable prose.
But I want to end where the novel's tragedy is quietly assembled — in the accumulated weight of decisions that cannot be undone.
Mr Tulliver's impulsive choices, Tom's inherited rigidities, Maggie's foreclosed futures.
Eleanor, you've been thinking about the way Eliot constructs Tulliver's fateful logic — that extraordinary passage about skeins and threads.
Yes — and it's one of those moments where you feel Eliot catching herself mid-sentence in sheer delight at what she's noticed.
She's describing Tulliver's psychology — this pattern of rash action that seems to contradict his usual sense of life's complexity.
And then she pivots into this extraordinary image.

"it is really not improbable that there was a direct relation between these apparently contradictory phenomena, since I have observed that for getting a strong impression that a skein is tangled there is nothing like snatching hastily at a single thread."
The "I have observed" is everything there.
The narrator steps forward — not as God, but as someone who has lived and watched and drawn a careful conclusion.
And the skein image does double work — it describes Tulliver perfectly, and it implicates all of us who grab at single explanations.
And the specific thread Tulliver grabs is money — as it always is in this novel.
He's decided to repay Mrs Glegg's five hundred pounds — a spirited, impulsive gesture — and then immediately looks around for someone he can squeeze to fund it.
That someone is his sister's husband Moss — a man evidently already struggling, given that Eliot calls their farm "dilapidated" a few pages later.
What strikes me as the social historian here is how this chain of debt runs always downward.
Tulliver feels the pressure from Mrs Glegg above him, and transfers it immediately to Moss below him.
The novel understands provincial financial life with a precision that most historians would envy.
But what undoes me is what happens when he actually rides away from the Moss farm.
Eliot gives us this image of him stopping his horse in the lane — turning his head from side to side in what she calls "a melancholy way."
And then he speaks aloud to no one.
"Poor little wench! she'll have nobody but Tom, belike, when I'm gone."
Six words — "she'll have nobody but Tom" — and the whole tragedy is there in miniature.
He loves her completely and has already imagined her future correctly — and still he cannot protect her from the very structures he is himself perpetuating.
That line is devastating precisely because of its dialect plainness.
"Belike" — that old-fashioned probabilistic hedge — makes it sound almost resigned rather than fearful.
And Eliot has set it up so carefully — "he appeared to be smitten by some sudden thought" — the passive construction makes it feel like fate arriving rather than reflection occurring.
Which connects directly to what Eliot does with him later — the Oedipus passage.
Yes — and that passage earns its weight.
Eliot establishes the irony clinically: Tulliver swears the loan must come from no client of Wakem's.
And then — the formulation is spare and exact — she writes:
"not because Mr Tulliver's will was feeble, but because external fact was stronger."
That sentence is doing extraordinary legal and philosophical work simultaneously.
It exonerates and condemns at once — this man is not weak, he is simply outgunned by circumstance.
And then comes the Oedipus comparison — which she refuses to make ironic.
"Mr Tulliver had a destiny as well as Œdipus, and in this case he might plead, like Œdipus, that his deed was inflicted on him rather than committed by him."
A provincial miller standing alongside Sophocles — and Eliot means it entirely seriously.
That seriousness is what first broke my heart in this novel.
She asks us to mourn a man who is stubborn, sometimes foolish, sometimes unjust to his own family.
And we do.
But of course what perpetuates the damage isn't Tulliver himself — it's Tom, carrying the prejudice forward.
Eliot is ruthless about exactly how that inheritance works.

"Let a prejudice be bequeathed, carried in the air, adopted by hearsay, caught in through the eye,—however it may come, these minds will give it a habitation; it is something to assert strongly and bravely, something to fill up the void of spontaneous ideas."
"Caught in through the eye" — as if prejudice were an infection, something that enters before the mind can close against it.
The grammar of that list is so deliberate — "bequeathed, carried, adopted, caught" — past participles accumulating like evidence at a trial.
And "fill up the void of spontaneous ideas" — that is Eliot at her most surgically honest about minds like Tom's.
He isn't evil.
He is rigidly, earnestly, catastrophically certain — and certainty is what destroys Maggie.
And Eliot gives Tom his own version of dignity in that — he calls it "duty to his father's memory" and "every manly feeling."
Those are not hollow phrases to Tom.
They are the load-bearing structure of his entire self.
Which is precisely why they cannot bend — and why Maggie cannot survive them.
It is perhaps the most painful irony the novel constructs — that the people who love Maggie most completely are also the ones who cannot let her live.
Her father sees her future with terrible clarity, and still the machinery grinds on.
Tom inherits not just the mill but the grievance — and makes it the whole architecture of his honour.
This is what it means, Eliot seems to say, to live in history rather than above it.
My profound thanks to Eleanor Hartley, James Blackstone, and Caroline Woodcourt — whose company through this novel has been a genuine pleasure.
And to our listeners — if you haven't yet read The Mill on the Floss, I hope we've given you sufficient reason.
If you have, I hope we've sent you back to it.

c3:p79.text:
Plotting covetousness and deliberate contrivance, in order to compass a selfish
end, are nowhere abundant but in the world of the dramatist: they demand too
intense a mental action for many of our fellow-parishioners to be guilty of
them. It is easy enough to spoil the lives of our neighbours without taking so
much trouble; we can do it by lazy acquiescence and lazy omission, by trivial
falsities for which we hardly know a reason, by small frauds neutralised by
small extravagances, by maladroit flatteries, and clumsily improvised
insinuations. We live from hand to mouth, most of us, with a small family of
immediate desires; we do little else than snatch a morsel to satisfy the hungry
brood, rarely thinking of seed-corn or the next year’s crop.
c3:p79.summary: The narrator offers profound reflection that most moral failures result not from deliberate villainy but from small, thoughtless acts, lazy compliance, and accumulated minor dishonestries.
c3:p79.best_quote: It is easy enough to spoil the lives of our neighbours without taking so much trouble; we can do it by lazy acquiescence and lazy omission, by trivial falsities for which we hardly know a reason, by small frauds neutralised by small extravagances, by maladroit flatteries, and clumsily improvised insinuations

c28:p64.text:
“Say no more, Tom, say no more; I’ve had enough for this day. Give
me a kiss, Bessy, and let us bear one another no ill-will; we shall never be
young again—this world’s been too many for me.”
c28:p64.summary: Mr Tulliver asks Tom to cease arguing, seeks reconciliation with his wife, and acknowledges that he and they are broken by forces beyond their control.
c28:p64.best_quote: we shall never be young again—this world's been too many for me

c37:p53.text:
“Do what  I  require,” said Tom. “I can’t trust
you, Maggie. There is no consistency in you. Put your hand on this Bible, and
say, ‘I renounce all private speech and intercourse with Philip Wakem
from this time forth.’ Else you will bring shame on us all, and grief on
my father; and what is the use of my exerting myself and giving up everything
else for the sake of paying my father’s debts, if you are to bring
madness and vexation on him, just when he might be easy and hold up his head
once more?”
c37:p53.summary: Tom insists Maggie must put her hand on the Bible and speak the exact words of renunciation, claiming he cannot trust her, that she lacks consistency, and that while he has been working to pay their father's debts and restore family respectability, she has done everything to destroy both.
c37:p53.best_quote: I can't trust you, Maggie. There is no consistency in you... while I have been contriving and working that my father may have some peace of mind before he dies,—working for the respectability of our family,—you have done all you can to destroy both

c11:p34.text:
Maggie Tulliver, you perceive, was by no means that well trained, well-informed
young person that a small female of eight or nine necessarily is in these days;
she had only been to school a year at St Ogg’s, and had so few books
that she sometimes read the dictionary; so that in travelling over her small
mind you would have found the most unexpected ignorance as well as unexpected
knowledge. She could have informed you that there was such a word as
“polygamy,” and being also acquainted with
“polysyllable,” she had deduced the conclusion that
“poly” mean “many”; but she had had no idea that
gypsies were not well supplied with groceries, and her thoughts generally were
the oddest mixture of clear-eyed acumen and blind dreams.
c11:p34.summary: The narrator reflects on Maggie's unusual, self-taught education: sophisticated in etymology and moral philosophy but naive about practical realities.
c11:p34.best_quote: in travelling over her small mind you would have found the most unexpected ignorance as well as unexpected knowledge.

c11:p0.text:
Maggie’s intentions, as usual, were on a larger scale than Tom imagined.
The resolution that gathered in her mind, after Tom and Lucy had walked away,
was not so simple as that of going home. No! she would run away and go to the
gypsies, and Tom should never see her any more. That was by no means a new idea
to Maggie; she had been so often told she was like a gypsy, and “half
wild,” that when she was miserable it seemed to her the only way of
escaping opprobrium, and being entirely in harmony with circumstances, would be
to live in a little brown tent on the commons; the gypsies, she considered,
would gladly receive her and pay her much respect on account of her superior
knowledge. She had once mentioned her views on this point to Tom and suggested
that he should stain his face brown, and they should run away together; but Tom
rejected the scheme with contempt, observing that gypsies were thieves, and
hardly got anything to eat and had nothing to drive but a donkey. To-day
however, Maggie thought her misery had reached a pitch at which gypsydom was
her refuge, and she rose from her seat on the roots of the tree with the sense
that this was a great crisis in her life; she would run straight away till she
came to Dunlow Common, where there would certainly be gypsies; and cruel Tom,
and the rest of her relations who found fault with her, should never see her
any more. She thought of her father as she ran along, but she reconciled
herself to the idea of parting with him, by determining that she would secretly
send him a letter by a small gypsy, who would run away without telling where
she was, and just let him know that she was well and happy, and always loved
him very much.
c11:p0.summary: Maggie resolves to run away to the gypsies after Tom's rejection, a fantasy she has long harboured as a way to escape family reproach and find harmony with her perceived wild nature.
c11:p0.best_quote: No! she would run away and go to the gypsies, and Tom should never see her any more.

c11:p35.text:
Her ideas about the gypsies had undergone a rapid modification in the last five
minutes. From having considered them very respectful companions, amenable to
instruction, she had begun to think that they meant perhaps to kill her as soon
as it was dark, and cut up her body for gradual cooking; the suspicion crossed
her that the fierce-eyed old man was in fact the Devil, who might drop that
transparent disguise at any moment, and turn either into the grinning
blacksmith, or else a fiery-eyed monster with dragon’s wings. It was no
use trying to eat the stew, and yet the thing she most dreaded was to offend
the gypsies, by betraying her extremely unfavourable opinion of them; and she
wondered, with a keenness of interest that no theologian could have exceeded,
whether, if the Devil were really present, he would know her thoughts.
c11:p35.summary: Maggie's fantasy collapses into paranoid horror as she imagines the gypsies as cannibals and the fierce-eyed man as the Devil.
c11:p35.best_quote: she had begun to think that they meant perhaps to kill her as soon as it was dark, and cut up her body for gradual cooking.

c10:p1.text:
Maggie said nothing, but turned away from her with a deeper frown. As long as
Tom seemed to prefer Lucy to her, Lucy made part of his unkindness. Maggie
would have thought a little while ago that she could never be cross with pretty
little Lucy, any more than she could be cruel to a little white mouse; but
then, Tom had always been quite indifferent to Lucy before, and it had been
left to Maggie to pet and make much of her. As it was, she was actually
beginning to think that she should like to make Lucy cry by slapping or
pinching her, especially as it might vex Tom, whom it was of no use to slap,
even if she dared, because he didn’t mind it. And if Lucy hadn’t
been there, Maggie was sure he would have got friends with her sooner.
c10:p1.summary: Maggie's jealousy transforms her affection into potential cruelty; she blames Lucy for Tom's unkindness and fantasizes about hurting her to vex Tom.
c10:p1.best_quote: Maggie would have thought a little while ago that she could never be cross with pretty little Lucy, any more than she could be cruel to a little white mouse; but then, Tom had always been quite indifferent to Lucy before, and it had been left to Maggie to pet and make much of her.

c14:p100.text:
But when this small apparatus of shallow quickness was fetched away in the gig
by Luke, and the study was once more quite lonely for Tom, he missed her
grievously. He had really been brighter, and had got through his lessons
better, since she had been there; and she had asked Mr Stelling so many
questions about the Roman Empire, and whether there really ever was a man who
said, in Latin, “I would not buy it for a farthing or a rotten
nut,” or whether that had only been turned into Latin, that Tom had
actually come to a dim understanding of the fact that there had once been
people upon the earth who were so fortunate as to know Latin without learning
it through the medium of the Eton Grammar. This luminous idea was a great
addition to his historical acquirements during this half-year, which were
otherwise confined to an epitomised history of the Jews.
c14:p100.summary: Tom grieves Maggie's departure and credits her insightful questions about the Roman Empire with expanding his historical understanding beyond his textbooks.
c14:p100.best_quote: he had actually come to a dim understanding of the fact that there had once been people upon the earth who were so fortunate as to know Latin without learning it through the medium of the Eton Grammar

c28:p29.text: “Ay, my little wench, but I shall never live twice o’er.”
c28:p29.summary: Mr Tulliver tells Maggie that even though she loves him, he will never have another chance at life or redemption.
c28:p29.best_quote: Ay, my little wench, but I shall never live twice o'er

c13:p5.text:
Mrs Glegg being in this state of satisfaction in her own lofty magnanimity, I
leave you to judge what effect was produced on her by the reception of a short
letter from Mr Tulliver that very evening, after Mrs Pullet’s
departure, informing her that she needn’t trouble her mind about her five
hundred pounds, for it should be paid back to her in the course of the next
month at farthest, together with the interest due thereon until the time of
payment. And furthermore, that Mr Tulliver had no wish to behave uncivilly to
Mrs Glegg, and she was welcome to his house whenever she liked to come, but he
desired no favours from her, either for himself or his children.
c13:p5.summary: Mr Tulliver writes to Mrs Glegg announcing he will repay her five hundred pounds within a month and neither desires nor requires her favours, completely inverting her anticipated reconciliation.
c13:p5.best_quote: she was welcome to his house whenever she liked to come, but he desired no favours from her, either for himself or his children.

c15:p18.text:
Mrs Tulliver, as we have seen, was not without influence over her husband. No
woman is; she can always incline him to do either what she wishes, or the
reverse; and on the composite impulses that were threatening to hurry Mr
Tulliver into “law,” Mrs Tulliver’s monotonous pleading had
doubtless its share of force; it might even be comparable to that proverbial
feather which has the credit or discredit of breaking the camel’s back;
though, on a strictly impartial view, the blame ought rather to lie with the
previous weight of feathers which had already placed the back in such imminent
peril that an otherwise innocent feather could not settle on it without
mischief. Not that Mrs Tulliver’s feeble beseeching could have had this
feather’s weight in virtue of her single personality; but whenever she
departed from entire assent to her husband, he saw in her the representative of
the Dodson family; and it was a guiding principle with Mr Tulliver to let the
Dodsons know that they were not to domineer over  him , or—more
specifically—that a male Tulliver was far more than equal to four female
Dodsons, even though one of them was Mrs Glegg.
c15:p18.summary: The narrator observes that Mrs Tulliver's weak pleading against law has cumulative force when combined with his fear of Dodson influence, though she is not powerful in herself.

c15:p19.text:
But not even a direct argument from that typical Dodson female herself against
his going to law could have heightened his disposition toward it so much as the
mere thought of Wakem, continually freshened by the sight of the too able
attorney on market-days. Wakem, to his certain knowledge, was (metaphorically
speaking) at the bottom of Pivart’s irrigation; Wakem had tried to make
Dix stand out, and go to law about the dam; it was unquestionably Wakem who had
caused Mr Tulliver to lose the suit about the right of road and the bridge
that made a thoroughfare of his land for every vagabond who preferred an
opportunity of damaging private property to walking like an honest man along
the highroad; all lawyers were more or less rascals, but Wakem’s
rascality was of that peculiarly aggravated kind which placed itself in
opposition to that form of right embodied in Mr Tulliver’s interests and
opinions. And as an extra touch of bitterness, the injured miller had recently,
in borrowing the five hundred pounds, been obliged to carry a little business
to Wakem’s office on his own account. A hook-nosed glib fellow! as cool
as a cucumber,—always looking so sure of his game! And it was vexatious
that Lawyer Gore was not more like him, but was a bald, round-featured man,
with bland manners and fat hands; a game-cock that you would be rash to bet
upon against Wakem. Gore was a sly fellow. His weakness did not lie on the side
of scrupulosity; but the largest amount of winking, however significant, is not
equivalent to seeing through a stone wall; and confident as Mr Tulliver was in
his principle that water was water, and in the direct inference that Pivart had
not a leg to stand on in this affair of irrigation, he had an uncomfortable
suspicion that Wakem had more law to show against this (rationally)
irrefragable inference than Gore could show for it. But then, if they went to
law, there was a chance for Mr Tulliver to employ Counsellor Wylde on his
side, instead of having that admirable bully against him; and the prospect of
seeing a witness of Wakem’s made to perspire and become confounded, as
Mr Tulliver’s witness had once been, was alluring to the love of
retributive justice.
c15:p19.summary: The narrator details Mr Tulliver's bitter conviction that Wakem orchestrates all his legal troubles and has humiliated him repeatedly; reveals his visceral hatred of the lawyer.
c15:p19.best_quote: A hook-nosed glib fellow! as cool as a cucumber,—always looking so sure of his game!

c25:p73.text:
Their mother came in now, and Maggie rushed away, that her burst of tears,
which she felt must come, might not happen till she was safe upstairs. They
were very bitter tears; everybody in the world seemed so hard and unkind to
Maggie; there was no indulgence, no fondness, such as she imagined when she
fashioned the world afresh in her own thoughts. In books there were people who
were always agreeable or tender, and delighted to do things that made one
happy, and who did not show their kindness by finding fault. The world outside
the books was not a happy one, Maggie felt; it seemed to be a world where
people behaved the best to those they did not pretend to love, and that did not
belong to them. And if life had no love in it, what else was there for Maggie?
Nothing but poverty and the companionship of her mother’s narrow griefs,
perhaps of her father’s heart-cutting childish dependence. There is no
hopelessness so sad as that of early youth, when the soul is made up of wants,
and has no long memories, no superadded life in the life of others; though we
who looked on think lightly of such premature despair, as if our vision of the
future lightened the blind sufferer’s present.
c25:p73.summary: Maggie rushes upstairs with bitter tears, feeling the world is hard and unkind; the narrator reveals her anguish: she expected love and tenderness from others as she imagines from books, but finds a harsh world where affection shows itself as fault-finding, and she sees no hope without love.

c52:p2.text:
Maggie, all this time, moved about with a quiescence and even torpor of manner,
so contrasted with her usual fitful brightness and ardor, that Lucy would have
had to seek some other cause for such a change, if she had not been convinced
that the position in which Maggie stood between Philip and her brother, and the
prospect of her self-imposed wearisome banishment, were quite enough to account
for a large amount of depression. But under this torpor there was a fierce
battle of emotions, such as Maggie in all her life of struggle had never known
or foreboded; it seemed to her as if all the worst evil in her had lain in
ambush till now, and had suddenly started up full-armed, with hideous,
overpowering strength! There were moments in which a cruel selfishness seemed
to be getting possession of her; why should not Lucy, why should not Philip,
suffer?  She  had had to suffer through many years of her life; and who
had renounced anything for her? And when something like that fulness of
existence—love, wealth, ease, refinement, all that her nature
craved—was brought within her reach, why was she to forego it, that
another might have it,—another, who perhaps needed it less? But amidst
all this new passionate tumult there were the old voices making themselves
heard with rising power, till, from time to time, the tumult seemed quelled.
 Was  that existence which tempted her the full existence she dreamed?
Where, then, would be all the memories of early striving; all the deep pity for
another’s pain, which had been nurtured in her through years of affection
and hardship; all the divine presentiment of something higher than mere
personal enjoyment, which had made the sacredness of life? She might as well
hope to enjoy walking by maiming her feet, as hope to enjoy an existence in
which she set out by maiming the faith and sympathy that were the best organs
of her soul. And then, if pain were so hard to  her , what was it to
others? “Ah, God! preserve me from inflicting—give me strength to
bear it.” How had she sunk into this struggle with a temptation that she
would once have thought herself as secure from as from deliberate crime? When
was that first hateful moment in which she had been conscious of a feeling that
clashed with her truth, affection, and gratitude, and had not shaken it from
her with horror, as if it had been a loathsome thing? And yet, since this
strange, sweet, subduing influence did not, should not, conquer
her,—since it was to remain simply her own suffering,—her mind was
meeting Stephen’s in that thought of his, that they might still snatch
moments of mute confession before the parting came. For was not he suffering
too? She saw it daily—saw it in the sickened look of fatigue with which,
as soon as he was not compelled to exert himself, he relapsed into indifference
toward everything but the possibility of watching her. Could she refuse
sometimes to answer that beseeching look which she felt to be following her
like a low murmur of love and pain? She refused it less and less, till at last
the evening for them both was sometimes made of a moment’s mutual gaze;
they thought of it till it came, and when it had come, they thought of nothing
else.
c52:p2.summary: Maggie experiences an unprecedented internal battle between cruel selfish impulses and her moral conscience, as the narrator reveals her struggle between personal happiness and loyalty to Lucy and Philip through a passage of intense philosophical introspection.
c52:p2.best_quote: "She might as well hope to enjoy walking by maiming her feet, as hope to enjoy an existence in which she set out by maiming the faith and sympathy that were the best organs of her soul."

c54:p7.text:
“You will find no home with me,” he answered, with tremulous rage.
“You have disgraced us all. You have disgraced my father’s name.
You have been a curse to your best friends. You have been base, deceitful; no
motives are strong enough to restrain you. I wash my hands of you forever. You
don’t belong to me.”

c5:p78.text:
It was one of their happy mornings. They trotted along and sat down together,
with no thought that life would ever change much for them; they would only get
bigger and not go to school, and it would always be like the holidays; they
would always live together and be fond of each other. And the mill with its
booming; the great chestnut-tree under which they played at houses; their own
little river, the Ripple, where the banks seemed like home, and Tom was always
seeing the water-rats, while Maggie gathered the purple plumy tops of the
reeds, which she forgot and dropped afterward; above all, the great Floss,
along which they wandered with a sense of travel, to see the rushing
spring-tide, the awful Eagre, come up like a hungry monster, or to see the
Great Ash which had once wailed and groaned like a man, these things would
always be just the same to them. Tom thought people were at a disadvantage who
lived on any other spot of the globe; and Maggie, when she read about
Christiana passing “the river over which there is no bridge,”
always saw the Floss between the green pastures by the Great Ash.
c5:p78.summary: The children imagine their happiness is eternal and unchanging; they associate the River Floss, the mill, and the landscape with home and permanence.
c5:p78.best_quote: They trotted along and sat down together, with no thought that life would ever change much for them; they would only get bigger and not go to school, and it would always be like the holidays; they would always live together and be fond of each other.

c5:p3.text:
Nevertheless he submitted to be kissed willingly enough, though Maggie hung on
his neck in rather a strangling fashion, while his blue-gray eyes wandered
toward the croft and the lambs and the river, where he promised himself that he
would begin to fish the first thing to-morrow morning. He was one of those lads
that grow everywhere in England, and at twelve or thirteen years of age look as
much alike as goslings,—a lad with light-brown hair, cheeks of cream and
roses, full lips, indeterminate nose and eyebrows,—a physiognomy in which
it seems impossible to discern anything but the generic character to boyhood;
as different as possible from poor Maggie’s phiz, which Nature seemed to
have moulded and coloured with the most decided intention. But that same Nature
has the deep cunning which hides itself under the appearance of openness, so
that simple people think they can see through her quite well, and all the while
she is secretly preparing a refutation of their confident prophecies. Under
these average boyish physiognomies that she seems to turn off by the gross, she
conceals some of her most rigid, inflexible purposes, some of her most
unmodifiable characters; and the dark-eyed, demonstrative, rebellious girl may
after all turn out to be a passive being compared with this pink-and-white bit
of masculinity with the indeterminate features.
c5:p3.summary: The narrator reflects on Tom's ordinary boyish appearance contrasted with Maggie's distinctive features, suggesting that Nature hides immutable character beneath superficial appearances.
c5:p3.best_quote: Under these average boyish physiognomies that she seems to turn off by the gross, she conceals some of her most rigid, inflexible purposes, some of her most unmodifiable characters
